claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has a hierarchical heterostructure featuring multilevel chemical fluctuations.
A physics-informed transformer combining microstructural descriptors and targeted DFT/CALPHAD outputs can accurately predict Young’s modulus for HfNbTiVAl10.
The proposed surrogate can accurately predict yield strength for HfNbTiVAl10.
The proposed surrogate can accurately predict fracture toughness for HfNbTiVAl10.
Hierarchical image descriptors combined with limited DFT/CALPHAD elastic constants provide an effective representation for predicting the three mechanical properties.
Active learning and data augmentation can make a limited HfNbTiVAl10 dataset capture broader variability in the hierarchical structure.
The proposed training regime requires an augmented dataset exceeding approximately 20–30 well-characterized HfNbTiVAl10 samples plus data from similar high-entropy alloys.
Transformer self-attention can learn complex relationships between microstructural features and macroscopic mechanical responses.
Pre-training on synthetic materials data and fine-tuning on HEA data can mitigate data scarcity and improve predictive accuracy.
Bayesian optimization and active learning will iteratively refine the model.
The surrogate approach will reduce reliance on extensive high-fidelity simulations.
The proposed model will reduce computational cost by approximately 90% relative to exhaustive DFT/CALPHAD simulations.
The proposed model will improve predictive accuracy by approximately 10–15% over prior methods.
Young’s modulus can be predicted with an error of approximately 5%.
Extensive physically based or high-fidelity calculations are computationally demanding.
Prior DFT/CALPHAD-based methods struggle to predict fracture toughness accurately.
Model reliability will diminish when the descriptors fail to represent unforeseen microstructural variations.
Rare phase events and processing-induced defects may lie outside the model’s reliable domain.
The model may become unreliable outside room-temperature tensile and specified fracture-test conditions.
Failure on a majority of blinded samples at errors above 5% for Young’s modulus or above 15% for yield strength and toughness would falsify the hypothesis.
